subtitle: The widely-used system that draws windows and manages graphics on workstations.

tldr.problem: Workstation software needed a standard way to draw windows, manage user input, and display graphics across different hardware.
tldr.mechanism: The MIT X Consortium published the X Window System specifications, a modular set of standards covering the protocol, libraries, toolkits and related technologies.
tldr.outcome: X became the dominant windowing system for Unix workstations in the 1980s and 1990s, and its architecture influenced GUI design for decades.

facts.label: Content
facts.value: Reference to MIT X Consortium standards

today: RFC 1198 is informational and remains a historical reference to the X Window System standards published by the MIT X Consortium. X Window System is still used today, particularly on Unix and Linux systems, though it has been complemented and partially superseded by other display servers like Wayland.

sections.title: The X Window System Standards
sections.content:
RFC 1198 is a reference document that points to the published standards of the MIT X Consortium for the X Window System. Rather than defining new specifications itself, it serves as a guide to where the official X standards live.

The standards cover the complete X Window System, from the low-level network protocol that sends drawing commands from client applications to an X server, to the high-level programming libraries and toolkits that application developers use.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is like a table of contents that tells you where to find the official rulebooks for X Window System.

sections.title: The X Architecture and Components
sections.content:
X Window System uses a client-server architecture where a client application sends requests to an X server, which manages the display, keyboard and mouse on a workstation. This design allows applications running on remote computers to display on a local screen over the network.

The standards encompass the X Protocol (the network messages), Xlib (a C language library), the X Toolkit Intrinsics (for building graphical interfaces), font conventions, the Display Manager for login sessions, shape extensions for non-rectangular windows, and draft standards for 3D graphics with PEX.
sections.plainLanguage: X separates the program from the screen. A program can ask a distant X server to draw pictures, so one computer can show what another computer is doing.

sections.title: Availability and Distribution
sections.content:
The MIT X software distribution was generally included with X Consortium implementations and was available via anonymous FTP from many sites around the world. The RFC lists contact information for the MIT Software Distribution Center, which could provide the distribution on tape for a nominal charge.

Questions about FTP sites and distribution were directed to xrequest@expo.lcs.mit.edu, and the MIT X Consortium Director could be reached at the Laboratory for Computer Science at MIT.
sections.plainLanguage: The X software was shared freely over the Internet, and you could also order it on tape from MIT.
